newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: BP sees short-term profit rise in Piedemonte.
newsitem.headline: BP sees short-term profit rise in Piedemonte.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc welcomed a decision Thursday by the Colombian authorities that should boost the short-term profitability of the Piedemonte block in eastern Colombia.

Under the terms of the existing sliding scale association contract that BP signed with state-run oil company Ecopetrol, BP's share of the profits falls from 50 percent to 30 percent as output increases.
Under the existing contract, Ecopetrol's share of the profits rise as production increases from 50 percent to a maximum 76 percent.

But the government Council of State earlier this week clarified the terms of the contract, ruling that the reserves, which are virtually all condensates according to BP, should be considered as gas rather than crude oil.

In practise this means BP will retain a higher share of profits over a longer period before dropping to the 30-70 percent split in favor of Ecopetrol, working on the ratio of 7,000 cubic feet of gas to one barrel of crude.
"We're assessing exactly what this ruling means but it will improve profitability in the short term for those formations already discovered," a senior BP official said.
"This will in the short term take BP's profitability to a good level in international terms," he added.

A spokeswoman for the Mines and Energy Ministry said the ruling came against the backdrop of a thorough review of the Piedemonte contract terms, adding: "This improves the profitability for BP a great deal even under the terms of the sliding scale contract."
The long-running debate over the Piedemonte block began when BP said that difficult drilling conditions cut potential profit margins to unacceptably low levels.

Estimated reserves in the three hydrocarbon formations so far discovered in the area are put at between 600 million and one billion barrels of condensates. But much of the 287,000 hectare block remains unexplored and could yield far higher reserves.

The short term boost for BP, however, is unlikely to resolve the issue of contract terms for the rest of the block. BP has said it hopes negotiations on improved contract terms for the estimated 85 percent not yet explored will provide the platform for the British multinational's long-term furute in Colombia.
"I'm not sure how this clarification fits into the overall Pidemonte discussions but we must assess what implications it has for a long-term equitable solution," the BP official said.
